strengths: Original and intuitive framing: learning vocabulary-integrated soft tokens as representations of procedural skills is a promising bridge between prompt tuning, continual learning, and compositional generalization.

The paper clearly defines three desired properties—frozen base weights, transfer to held-out skill combinations, and zero-shot composition of independently learned skills—and organizes the experiments around them.

The controlled digit-transformation environment permits explicit skill annotations and clean ID/OOD composition splits. Testing all operation orderings and separately holding out each pretrained operation are useful design choices.

Figures 4 and A2 show a sizeable and fairly consistent OOD advantage over the implemented prompt-tuning and LoRA baselines, while the token-length and training-complexity ablations provide useful evidence about when the method works.

The writing and visual presentation are generally clear, and the appendix reports many important implementation details, including data sizes, hyperparameters, trainable-parameter counts, hardware, and evaluation-set construction.

The limitations section appropriately acknowledges the synthetic scope, dependence on skill-centered data, soft-token optimization sensitivity, proximity to pretrained capabilities, and backpropagation cost. The synthetic experiments present no substantial research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: The evidence is too narrow for the central continual-learning claims: all main results use one specially LoRA-pretrained 0.5B model, two new operations, and one synthetic digit domain. There is no natural-language, code, tool-use, standard pretrained-model, or longer skill-stream experiment, and no evaluation of accumulating many skills, interference, storage growth, token collisions, or retention. The results therefore establish a toy proof of concept rather than a scalable path to continual learning.

The decisive Property 3 comparison is incomplete. The paper asserts that independently trained prompt-tuning prefixes are structurally unable to compose, but concatenating or otherwise combining two independently trained prefixes is mechanically possible and should be tested. Figure 5 instead compares only against ICL, which receives raw examples and is not a parameter-matched modular adaptation baseline. Thus the experiment does not isolate whether vocabulary-level placement enables composition.

The method-versus-prompt-tuning comparison confounds vocabulary integration with token position and prompt structure: the proposed tokens replace operation markers at their semantic locations, whereas the prompt-tuning tokens form a prefix. Controls placing ordinary learned soft tokens at the same locations, moving neologisms to a prefix, or varying insertion position are needed before attributing the gain to vocabulary-level integration.

Statistical support is weak. Most reported variation is across different held-out operations, not independent training seeds, and several ablations appear to use single runs. Consequently, the substantial initialization variability in Table A2 and the robustness of the headline gaps cannot be assessed. Figure 5 also compares variation over six held-out-training configurations against variation over four different ICL context sizes, which are not comparable uncertainty estimates.

The multi-skill experiment is small and somewhat artificial: it combines only two related, deterministic transformations, evaluates just 50 samples per sequence length, and averages replicas trained under different but evaluation-irrelevant held-out operations. Accuracy is already below 0.6 at length 2 and falls near 0.2 by length 8, tempering the claim that the skills are composed “successfully.”

The Section 4 evidence does not establish that individual pretrained vocabulary tokens encode procedural knowledge. “XOR” may tokenize into multiple pieces, the keyword changes the semantic instruction, and the natural-language-description control is awkwardly phrased. With only 100 samples, no prompt paraphrases, and no tokenization or causal embedding intervention, the frequency-based interpretation remains speculative.

Reproducibility is only partial: detailed configurations are supplied, but no code, generated datasets, checkpoints, random seeds, software versions, or per-seed results are provided. Some protocol choices also require clarification, including the temperature-1 setting in Table E3 versus greedy evaluation elsewhere and precisely how multiple 20-token neologisms are ordered when replacing operation labels.

The related-work argument overstates structural limitations of alternative modular methods. Composable adapters, mixtures, and simple concatenation controls deserve empirical treatment; higher-capacity LoRA is also not a parameter-matched baseline, so its worse OOD behavior does not by itself demonstrate an advantage inherent to neologisms.

Presentation is readable but contains numerous grammatical errors and a few underspecified or inconsistent descriptions. A short discussion of misuse or safety implications of portable learned skill tokens would also improve the otherwise low-risk ethics treatment.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and intuitively appealing formulation of skill-based continual learning through three properties: frozen base weights, transfer to held-out skill combinations, and composition of independently learned skills.

The controlled digit-transformation environment makes skill membership and ID/OOD composition splits explicit. Testing all operation-order permutations is a useful precaution against memorizing a single canonical ordering.

The appendices report many implementation details, including training-set sizes, model and LoRA configurations, learning rates, batch sizes, hardware, and per-held-out-skill results. The token-length, training-complexity, and initialization ablations are informative.

The manuscript is visually polished and includes an appropriately candid limitations section covering synthetic-only evidence, skill-centered data requirements, soft-token instability, and computational cost. The synthetic experiments raise no material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central evidence is confined to a bespoke Qwen2.5-0.5B model trained on a tiny synthetic transformation language, with only two nominally new operations. The insertion function replaces an operation symbol at exactly the semantic location where the task-trained model expects an operator. This principally demonstrates new-operator embedding learning in a toy DSL, not scalable continual learning in realistic LLM settings.

Soundness: The Prompt Tuning comparison confounds integration location with the claimed skill-centric representation: Skill Neologisms replace the target operator inside the expression, whereas Prompt Tuning places the same number of vectors before the prompt. An insertion-matched soft-token baseline is missing, so Figure 4 does not isolate whether vocabulary integration, position, or simple access to the model's learned operator slot causes the gain.

Soundness: Property 3 is not established against the most important baseline. The paper asserts that independently trained prompt prefixes cannot be composed, but never tests concatenating or otherwise combining the independently trained Prompt Tuning vectors. Figure 5 instead compares against ICL, uses only one pair of new skills, reports fairly low absolute accuracy, and supplies neither a jointly trained upper bound nor single-skill controls. Existing ways of composing LoRA adapters also make the blanket claim of structural impossibility too strong.

Soundness: INV-POL is not convincingly a new capability: on the stated modulo-10 domain it is exactly obtainable by applying ADD (or SUB) followed by the pretrained POL operation. Several held-out compositions are also degenerate or information-destroying, and holding out ID is a particularly weak OOD test. Averaging these heterogeneous cases obscures what kind of compositional generalization is occurring.

Soundness and statistical evidence: Results appear to use one optimization run per configuration. Reported standard deviations are across different held-out operations or ICL example counts rather than random seeds, despite acknowledged soft-token instability. There are no significance tests, and the sharp per-operation variation in the appendix indicates that seed-level robustness is important.

The Section 4 experiment does not demonstrate that individual vocabulary embeddings encode procedural knowledge. Adding the word 'XOR' changes the semantic instruction processed by the entire network; no tokenization analysis, embedding intervention, lexical controls, or paraphrase controls isolate the token embedding. The comparison with XNOR frequency is correlational, and the explicit-description prompt may itself be a weak or unnatural baseline.

Significance and originality: Learning input embeddings or pseudo-tokens for concepts, tools, prompts, and behaviors is well established. Skill-centered sampling and operator-position insertion are a plausible combination, but evidence from two synthetic operations is too narrow to substantiate the claimed path toward scalable skill-based continual learning or distinguish it decisively from prior soft-token adaptation.

Reproducibility: Although many hyperparameters are included, no code or generated datasets are provided, and important details such as optimizer, seeds, model revision, scheduling, decoding limits, and exact tokenization are missing. There is also a concrete inconsistency: Section 5.3.1 states 768 parameters per token and about 153k for 200 tokens, while Appendix E.8 reports embedding dimension 896, which would imply 896 and 179,200 parameters.

Presentation: The conceptual structure is clear, but claims repeatedly exceed the evidence—for example, that P2 and P3 are 'validated' and that the method provides a scalable continual-learning path. Smaller grammatical errors and inconsistent terminology further reduce polish. Overall, the promising proof of concept requires fairer baselines, repeated trials, non-degenerate skills, and substantially broader evaluation before others can reliably build on its conclusions.

strengths: Soundness: The controlled experiments support the paper's narrow claim that vocabulary-integrated soft tokens can learn composable digit transformations. Skill Neologisms substantially outperform parameter-matched Prompt Tuning on held-out two-skill compositions (average OOD accuracy 0.75 vs. 0.60 for SHIFT and 0.84 vs. 0.57 for INV-POL), with similar results for three-skill compositions.

The independently trained SHIFT and INV-POL tokens retain nontrivial accuracy when combined without joint training, directly demonstrating the proposed multi-skill composition property in this setting.

Originality and significance: Framing vocabulary-level soft tokens as reusable procedural-skill representations is a clear and interesting extension of prompt tuning and meaningful-token work. The distinction between task-centered and skill-centered training is useful and may stimulate further research on modular continual learning.

The ablations provide useful mechanistic evidence: OOD transfer improves with composition-rich training, excessively long neologisms generalize worse, and initialization from pretrained operation embeddings is helpful but not essential.

Presentation: The manuscript is well organized, motivates three concrete target properties, and uses an experimental domain in which skills and ID/OOD compositions can be defined unambiguously. Figures and tables are generally clear. The limitations discussion is appropriately candid about the synthetic proof-of-concept, dependence on skill-centered data, soft-token optimization sensitivity, applicability near the pretraining distribution, and training cost. The synthetic experiments raise no material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Significance and external validity are limited by evaluation on one specially pretrained 0.5B model, two new deterministic digit operations, and a grammar that already represents operations as tokens. Replacing an operator token with a learned embedding is particularly favorable to the proposed method; no natural-language, standard continual-learning, larger-model, or longer skill-sequence evaluation establishes that the approach scales to realistic skills.

The comparison with Prompt Tuning changes token position as well as the claimed semantic integration: the baseline places tokens at the prefix, whereas Skill Neologisms place them in the operator slot. Thus the results establish the benefit of this intervention as a package, but do not isolate whether vocabulary integration, semantically appropriate placement, or skill-centered training drives the gain. Stronger baselines should include position-matched soft tokens and other composable prompt/adaptor methods.

Statistical evidence is weak. Main experiments appear to use one optimization run per configuration, with variation reported across different held-out operations rather than independent seeds. This is important because the paper itself notes soft-token instability, and random initialization produces highly variable outcomes, including zero accuracy for some held-out operations.

The Figure 5 ICL comparison is not cleanly summarized: its mean and standard deviation aggregate four different demonstration counts (10, 20, 50, and 100), while the Skill Neologism band aggregates six held-out-skill configurations. These are heterogeneous conditions rather than repeated trials, so the claim of significant superiority lacks a statistical test and should not rely on these error bands. The learned method also uses 100,000 supervised samples per skill, making ICL chiefly a qualitative baseline.

The broad continual-learning framing is stronger than the demonstrated result. Freezing the base model does avoid direct forgetting, but the paper does not test a sequential stream, many accumulated skills, storage and routing as the vocabulary grows, interference among numerous neologisms, or retention of general capabilities. Accordingly, it supports a promising primitive for continual learning rather than a validated continual-learning system.

Reproducibility is only partial. The appendices report many hyperparameters and dataset-generation rules, but no code or generated data are provided, and random seeds, optimizer details, stopping/model-selection procedure, and repeated-run results are absent. There are also reporting inconsistencies: Section 5.3.1 calculates token parameters using dimension 768, although the stated Qwen2.5-0.5B embedding dimension is 896; Table E4 collapses the three max-operation settings into one row; and multi-skill inference uses temperature 1 despite otherwise emphasizing greedy evaluation.

The XOR/XNOR study is suggestive rather than decisive evidence that ordinary vocabulary tokens intrinsically encode procedural knowledge. It uses only 100 examples per condition, does not control for alternative phrasings or tokenization/frequency confounds, and the natural-language description may itself be harder for the tested models to apply.

strengths: Soundness: The controlled digit-transformation setting defines skills and held-out compositions precisely, and the results show a substantial OOD advantage over the implemented LoRA and prefix-tuning baselines.
Originality: Treating vocabulary-integrated soft tokens as independently learnable procedural representations is a simple, interesting extension of prompt tuning and meaningful-token research.

Significance: Zero-shot composition of separately trained capability modules would be valuable for modular adaptation and continual learning if it generalizes beyond the favorable proof-of-concept setting.
Presentation: The paper is clear, well organized, and unusually explicit about its three desired properties. Figures, algorithms, ablations, and appendices make the method easy to understand.
The capacity, composition-complexity, initialization, and label-noise studies provide useful preliminary insight rather than reporting only headline results.
The limitations section appropriately acknowledges reliance on skill-centered datasets, soft-token instability, pretraining proximity, and full-model backpropagation cost.
weaknesses: Soundness: The decisive comparisons do not isolate the claimed innovation. Skill neologisms are inserted at the semantic operator/name locations, whereas prompt-tuning tokens are placed only as a prefix. Thus the results confound vocabulary integration with token position and insertion function. A matched baseline inserting ordinary learned soft-prompt tokens at exactly the same positions is essential.

Property 3 is not tested against direct composition baselines. The paper asserts that independently trained prompts or adapters are structurally non-composable, but does not evaluate concatenated independently trained prompts, prompt mixtures, adapter merging/arithmetic, or related modular-composition methods. Only the proposed method is allowed to combine its two learned modules in Figures 5 and 7.

The continual-learning claim is substantially broader than the evidence. There is no sequential learning protocol, scaling study over many acquired skills, interference among a growing token library, routing or skill-selection evaluation, or memory/capacity analysis. Freezing the base model makes absence of forgetting largely true by construction, and only two new skills are learned.

The synthetic experiment is highly favorable: the base model is explicitly trained to compose symbolic operator tokens, and a new token replaces an operator at exactly the location where the model expects one. Results from this custom 0.5B model therefore provide limited evidence about acquiring realistic new capabilities in pretrained LLMs.

The natural-language validation covers one model, one benchmark, one pair of hand-selected low-performing skills, and only 50 stochastic test queries. It reports no random-seed variation, confidence intervals, human validation, or replication across skill pairs. GPT-5 generates the training answers and grades the outputs, introducing possible evaluator bias.

Figure 7's prompts retain definitions and examples of both requested skills even when their names are replaced by soft tokens. Consequently, it is unclear whether the tokens encode new procedural knowledge, improve attention to already supplied instructions, or exploit benchmark-specific formatting.

The evidence for naturally occurring procedural tokens in Section 4 is suggestive but under-controlled. The XOR-versus-XNOR comparison cannot separate procedural knowledge from token frequency, tokenization, prompt familiarity, or memorized conventional notation; synonym, frequency-matched, and random-token controls are absent.

Reproducibility is incomplete: random seeds and independent-run counts are not specified, several reported standard deviations aggregate heterogeneous held-out skills rather than training variability, the exact GPT-5 version is unspecified, and the generated natural-language training set is not included in the manuscript. The visible code links are also blank.

The impact statement is too cursory for a mechanism that can package opaque capabilities into transferable soft tokens. Risks involving auditability, capability sharing, misuse, and safety-control circumvention deserve discussion, even if they do not presently create a decisive ethical barrier.

strengths: The paper presents an intuitive and potentially useful idea: represent a procedural capability using a small set of trainable, vocabulary-integrated embeddings while freezing the pretrained parameters. Independently trained embeddings can then be placed together in one context.

The synthetic evaluation is thoughtfully constructed around explicit operations, leave-one-operation-out composition, multiple operation orders, and held-out sequence lengths. Skill neologisms substantially outperform ordinary prompt tuning and LoRA on the reported two-operation OOD test (Figure 4).

The paper includes useful ablations of token length, training-composition complexity, initialization, and label noise. In particular, the deterioration beyond 20 tokens and the benefit of composition-rich training provide actionable empirical observations.

The natural-language experiment offers promising preliminary evidence: independently trained tokens for modus ponens and statistical syllogism achieve about 70% joint success on Skill-Mix, compared with a very weak base model.

Presentation is generally clear and visually polished. The three desired properties are stated explicitly, experimental details and prompts are supplied in the appendix, and the limitations section candidly discusses dataset construction, optimization sensitivity, task proximity, and computational cost.
No serious ethical issue is apparent for the experiments as conducted; the work uses standard public models and largely synthetic or generated data.
weaknesses: The central continual-learning claim is not established. There is no sequential learning experiment, measurement of retention or catastrophic forgetting, study of interference as many skills accumulate, or composition of more than two newly learned skills. The evidence supports a small proof of concept for soft-token composition, not a scalable continual-learning method.

The asserted Property 1, “no weight updates,” is misleading: the method learns new embedding parameters, which are model weights in the ordinary sense. Moreover, the synthetic base model has tied input/output embeddings. Extending its vocabulary can introduce additional output logits and alter the softmax even when a skill token is absent, yet the paper never evaluates unchanged behavior on old tasks after vocabulary extension. Thus the claimed prevention of forgetting is not demonstrated.

The key comparison with prompt tuning is confounded by token placement. Prompt tokens are placed only as a prefix, whereas neologisms replace the operation marker at its semantically informative location. In Skill-Mix, every occurrence of a skill name is replaced, so the same 20-token sequence appears multiple times while the prompt-tuning baseline receives one 20-token prefix. A position-matched insertion baseline and controls for token repetitions/context length are needed before attributing the gain to “vocabulary-level integration.”

The claim that prompt tuning and LoRA are structurally unable to support independent composition is too strong. Concatenating independently learned prompts and merging or combining adapters are obvious baselines, with related composition methods already existing. The paper does not empirically attempt these baselines, and Figure 7 reports joint use only for neologisms.

The synthetic evidence is narrow: it uses one specially LoRA-trained Qwen2.5-0.5B model and only two added deterministic digit operations. Performance for composing the two learned operations is modest and falls from roughly 0.57 at length 2 to roughly 0.2 at length 8 (Figure 5). There are no results across base-model families, capacities, learned-skill counts, or substantially different algorithmic domains.

The natural-language validation is underpowered and potentially circular. It selects two skills, uses only 300 GPT-5-generated training examples per skill and 50 stochastic test prompts, and uses GPT-5 again as the sole judge without human validation, judge-reliability analysis, confidence intervals, or repeated training/evaluation seeds. The inference prompt also supplies a definition and example of every requested skill, making it unclear how much genuinely new procedural knowledge the tokens contain rather than merely steering generation toward a demonstrated format.

The “naturally occurring skill tokens” study does not justify its conclusion. The paper does not establish that XOR or XNOR is represented by a single tokenizer token in each model, and a keyword can retrieve distributed knowledge stored throughout the network without itself encapsulating procedural knowledge. The comparison uses only 100 three-bit examples and lacks tokenization checks, paraphrases, frequency-matched controls, or nonsense-token controls.

Reported uncertainty is inadequate. Most training configurations appear to use one random seed; standard deviations in the synthetic tables are across heterogeneous held-out operations rather than independent repetitions. Consequently, optimization stability and statistical significance cannot be assessed, despite soft-prompt instability being an acknowledged limitation.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript contains blank code links, does not provide generated datasets or individual Skill-Mix outputs/grades, and depends on the proprietary and evolving label “GPT-5” without a reproducible model snapshot. Hyperparameters are fairly detailed, but these omissions prevent faithful verification of the most realistic experiment.

The limitations and impact discussions omit several decisive concerns: the absence of actual continual-learning evaluation, scaling costs from adding 20 context tokens per skill, possible output-distribution changes under tied embeddings, unfair baseline placement, and misuse risks from portable capability tokens. These omissions matter more than the limitations the paper does acknowledge.

Overall, the idea and controlled results are promising, but important confounds and the large gap between the experiments and the headline claims prevent acceptance in the current form. A convincing revision would require position- and capacity-matched compositional baselines, multi-seed results, direct retention tests, sequential acquisition of many skills, and substantially broader natural-language evaluation.

strengths: Soundness: The controlled digit-transformation setup cleanly defines skills and permits meaningful leave-one-skill-out tests. Skill neologisms substantially outperform prompt tuning and LoRA on two-skill OOD composition (e.g., 0.75 versus 0.60 and 0.16 for SHIFT; 0.84 versus 0.57 and 0.28 for INV-POL), while all methods perform similarly in-distribution.

Significance: Learning modular capabilities without modifying the frozen base model is an important continual-learning direction. The demonstrated zero-shot composition of independently trained skill tokens is particularly promising.

Originality: Combining skill-centered training with vocabulary-integrated soft tokens is a conceptually simple but novel reframing of prompt tuning. The focus on independently composable procedural knowledge distinguishes the contribution from standard task-specific soft prompts.

Presentation: The paper is well organized, clearly defines its three desired properties, and uses helpful controlled experiments, detailed appendices, and ablations over token length, training-composition complexity, initialization, and label noise.

The Skill-Mix experiment provides encouraging evidence beyond the synthetic setting: independently learned tokens jointly achieve roughly 70% success on both skills, compared with about 6% for the base model. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges dataset construction, optimization sensitivity, scope, and computational cost.
Research ethics: The experiments present no major immediate ethical concern, and freezing the base model reduces one source of unintended capability degradation.
weaknesses: Soundness: The empirical scope remains narrow: the principal evidence uses two artificial target operations on one specially fine-tuned 0.5B model, while the natural-language evaluation uses only two selected skills, one model, 50 joint test queries, and apparently no independent training seeds. Variability across held-out operations is sometimes large, including near-total failures, so averages alone overstate reliability.

The decisive multi-skill experiment lacks the most direct baselines: concatenating independently trained prompt-tuning prefixes, prompt-composition methods such as ATTEMPT/MTP-style variants, and adapter-merging approaches. Claiming that prefixes or adapters are structurally unable to compose is too strong without testing such baselines; consequently, the evidence does not fully isolate vocabulary-level integration as the cause of the gain.

The Skill-Mix evidence relies on GPT-5 both to generate training answers and to grade outputs, with no human validation, alternative judge, judge-agreement analysis, confidence intervals, or repeated sampling. This creates possible generator/judge bias and makes the approximately 70% result less conclusive than the presentation suggests.

The paper is best viewed as a proof of concept rather than a demonstrated continual-learning system. It does not study long sequences of acquired skills, scaling in the number of stored or simultaneously composed skills, interference among many neologisms, token-management costs, or whether capability acquisition remains stable across model families.

Reproducibility is weakened by absent/redacted code links and internal inconsistencies: the main text states a 768-dimensional token embedding whereas Appendix D reports dimension 896 for Qwen2.5-0.5B, and the reported epoch counts differ between the main configuration and an ablation table. Dataset-generation and stochastic-replication details are also insufficient for exact reproduction.

The Section 4 XOR/XNOR study does not establish that particular vocabulary embeddings themselves encode procedural knowledge: ordinary semantic instruction-following and potentially multi-token tokenization are confounds. Embedding ablations or controlled token replacements would be needed for that mechanistic interpretation.

Presentation and ethics: Calling the method free of weight updates is potentially confusing because newly added embedding parameters are optimized; 'no base-model weight updates' would be more precise. The impact statement also overlooks that learned soft tokens could bypass behavioral safeguards or introduce hidden trigger-like behavior, even when the base weights remain frozen.
